planting.note: Direct sow or start transplants in early spring; Ishikura can also be sown in late summer for a fall and winter harvest in zone 9. Successive sowings every 3-4 weeks keep a steady supply of scallions coming.

directions: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart; hilling soil up around the base as plants grow blanches the shanks white and tender. Ishikura is a classic Japanese bunching onion, or negi, that forms a long, straight, pure-white shank without ever swelling into a bulb, staying tender and mild even as it grows tall. It is slow to bolt, tolerates both summer heat and winter cold well, and can be harvested at scallion size or left to mature into thick, leek-like stalks. Because it does not form a storage bulb, Ishikura is best used fresh, sliced into stir-fries, soups, and as a raw garnish; cut-and-come-again harvesting of the outer leaves extends the picking season from a single planting.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Bunching Onion Growing Guide

planting.note: Direct sow or start transplants in early spring; can also be sown in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9. Purple color develops best with cool temperatures and full sun.

directions: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart for straight, uniform stalks. Deep Purple is a non-bulbing bunching onion selected for shanks that flush a striking violet-purple, especially in cool weather, contrasting with its blue-green tops; the color makes it a standout in salads, garnishes, and pickles compared with standard green scallions. Flavor is typical mild-to-sharp onion, good raw or cooked, and the plant is otherwise grown exactly like any other bunching onion. Harvest at scallion size for the best color and tenderness, or let a portion mature further for thicker stalks; successive small sowings keep a continuous supply.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Onions

planting.note: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they root before winter; spring planting also works but establishes more slowly. Catawissa is a 19th-century American heirloom walking onion selection, distinct from the common Egyptian walking onion in its looser, more open topset clusters and occasional true flowers mixed among the bulbils.

directions: Plant topset bulbils 1-2 inches deep in well-drained soil in fall or early spring; established clumps are extremely low-maintenance and benefit from dividing every few years to maintain vigor. Catawissa is a historic American heirloom perennial onion, first documented in Pennsylvania in the 1800s, that produces clusters of small aerial bulbils atop tall seed stalks; as the topsets mature and become heavy, the stalk arches over and the bulbils root wherever they touch soil, letting the planting slowly spread, or 'walk', across the bed on its own. Compared with the more commonly sold Egyptian walking onion, Catawissa's topset clusters are looser and sometimes mixed with small true flowers, and some gardeners find its flavor slightly milder. Harvest green tops through the season like scallions, or dig the underground bulbs once foliage begins to die back; the aerial bulbils themselves can be pickled or used as new planting stock.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom onion archive
University of Illinois Extension — Perennial Onions

common_name: Hill Hardy Rosemary (Madalene Hill Cold-Hardy Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun, well-drained soil; Hill Hardy is one of the most cold-hardy rosemary selections available, tolerating temperatures well below the range that damages standard rosemary when grown in a sheltered, well-drained site.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; like other rosemary cultivars it dislikes rich, moisture-retentive soil, which encourages soft, frost-tender growth at the expense of cold hardiness. Hill Hardy is a cold-hardy rosemary selection associated with Madalene Hill, the pioneering Texas herb grower who also introduced Arp rosemary, and is prized alongside Arp as one of the more winter-tolerant named rosemary cultivars available to home gardeners in marginal climates. Its habit is semi-upright to spreading, somewhat looser than a compact culinary type, with the same piney, resinous fragrance and flavor as any standard rosemary, making it fully usable in the kitchen for roasting, grilling, and seasoning. Prune after flowering to maintain a dense, shapely plant, and avoid overwatering or heavy mulch against the crown, which invites root rot in humid Gulf South summers.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Herb Cultivar Notes
Festival Hill — Madalene Hill Herb Garden

common_name: Miss Jessopp's Upright Rosemary (Tall Hedging Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring in full sun, well-drained soil; Miss Jessopp's Upright is a classic English cultivar grown for its strongly vertical, columnar growth habit, making it a favorite for clipped hedges and formal topiary.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; avoid heavy, wet soils and overhead watering, which promote root and foliar disease. Miss Jessopp's Upright is a long-cultivated English rosemary selection prized for its tall, narrow, strongly vertical branching, which holds its shape naturally and makes it one of the best rosemary cultivars for clipped hedges, screens, and formal topiary shapes rather than a sprawling border plant. Culinary quality is excellent and identical in use to any standard rosemary — piney, resinous leaves for roasting, grilling, and seasoning — while pale blue flowers appear along the upright stems in late winter and spring, attracting bees. Prune after flowering to maintain a tight hedge form, and in zone 9 give it a warm, sheltered, sharply drained site, since it is somewhat less cold-hardy than selections like Arp or Hill Hardy.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Rosemary Cultivar Notes
North Carolina State University Extension — Rosemary Plant Profile
